title: Reading a Cell's Voltage and Its Currents
endLine: Record voltage from inside; hold it fixed to measure the currents.

scenes.tts: How can a cell look electrically still while currents pour across it? When its voltage spikes, how do you tell which ions drove it? Both answers start with a fine electrode inside the cell.
scenes.caption: How can a cell look electrically still while currents pour across it? When its voltage spikes, how do you tell which ions drove it? Both answers start with a fine electrode inside the cell.
scenes.visual: Carried world (schematic, filling at least 60% of frame height): left side shows a living cell cross-section with a smooth membrane band separating outside bath from inside cytoplasm, ion dots drifting gently on both sides; right side shows a flat live voltage trace. Opposing arrows pulse quietly across the membrane while the trace stays flat; then a schematic voltage spike rises on the trace as a fine glass electrode glides down toward the cell membrane.
scenes.narration: How can a cell look electrically still while currents pour across it? When its voltage spikes, how do you tell which ions drove it? Both answers start with a fine electrode inside the cell.

scenes.visual: The schematic cell cross-section and drifting ion dots dim slightly behind high-contrast title text: 'Reading a Cell's Voltage and Its Currents'. Ion dots keep drifting slowly.

scenes.tts: First, push a fine glass electrode inside the cell. Inside minus outside is the membrane potential. In a made-up neuron resting at minus seventy-one millivolts, the trace stays flat. Yet about two hundred picoamperes of potassium leave while two hundred of sodium enter. Equal currents cancel, hiding flow.
scenes.caption: First, push a fine glass electrode inside the cell. Inside minus outside is the membrane potential. In a made-up neuron resting at −71 mV, the trace stays flat. Yet about 200 picoamperes of potassium leave while 200 of sodium enter. Equal currents cancel, hiding flow.
scenes.visual: Same cell cross-section (schematic): the fine glass electrode pierces the membrane into the cytoplasm before the narrator names it. A simple label 'Inside − Outside' resolves to 'Membrane potential' as the right-hand trace settles flat at −71 mV (labeled 'Made-up neuron'). Two equal-sized current arrows animate simultaneously through simple schematic membrane pores: '200 pA K+ out' and '200 pA Na+ in', balancing so the −71 mV trace stays completely level.
scenes.narration: First, push a fine glass electrode inside the cell. Inside minus outside is the membrane potential. In a made-up neuron resting at −71 mV, the trace stays flat. Yet about 200 picoamperes of potassium leave while 200 of sodium enter. Equal currents cancel, hiding flow.

scenes.tts: Each ion has an equilibrium potential, where concentration push balances electrical pull. Driving force is membrane voltage minus that value. Our neuron's potassium value is minus ninety-five millivolts. Minus seventy-one sits twenty-four millivolts above it, so potassium is pushed out. If voltage moves, driving force moves, so current changes even when channels do not.
scenes.caption: Each ion has an equilibrium potential, where concentration push balances electrical pull. Driving force is membrane voltage minus that value. Our neuron's potassium value is −95 mV. −71 mV sits 24 mV above it, so potassium is pushed out. If voltage moves, driving force moves, so current changes even when channels do not.
scenes.visual: The right-hand trace panel morphs smoothly into a vertical voltage scale next to the same made-up cell (schematic, computed arithmetic): a mark settles at −95 mV labeled 'K+ equilibrium (E)' as opposing concentration and electrical arrows balance at that point. The formula 'Driving force = Vm − E' appears cleanly in large type. As spoken, the Vm marker lights at '−71 mV', a bracket spans the gap down to the −95 mV mark, and '−71 − (−95) = +24 mV' lights up with an outward potassium arrow. Then the Vm marker glides up and down freely while the driving-force bracket stretches and shrinks with it, the channel pores unchanged.
scenes.narration: Each ion has an equilibrium potential, where concentration push balances electrical pull. Driving force is membrane voltage minus that value. Our neuron's potassium value is −95 mV. −71 mV sits 24 mV above it, so potassium is pushed out. If voltage moves, driving force moves, so current changes even when channels do not.

scenes.tts: Voltage clamp breaks that tie by holding membrane voltage fixed. You pick a voltage, and the electrode injects whatever current keeps it there. That injected current matches the current crossing the membrane, so you measure it. With voltage fixed, driving force stays constant, so current changes track the channels themselves.
scenes.caption: Voltage clamp breaks that tie by holding membrane voltage fixed. You pick a voltage, and the electrode injects whatever current keeps it there. That injected current matches the current crossing the membrane, so you measure it. With voltage fixed, driving force stays constant, so current changes track the channels themselves.
scenes.visual: Same cell cross-section and right-hand panel (schematic): a clamp lock engages on the Vm marker, snapping the upper voltage trace to a clean flat step while a current-injection indicator pulses at the electrode. The driving-force bracket locks at a constant length. Directly below the flat voltage trace, a schematic current trace comes alive and moves in sync as simple schematic channel pores open and shut in the membrane.
scenes.narration: Voltage clamp breaks that tie by holding membrane voltage fixed. You pick a voltage, and the electrode injects whatever current keeps it there. That injected current matches the current crossing the membrane, so you measure it. With voltage fixed, driving force stays constant, so current changes track the channels themselves.

scenes.tts: Holding voltage fixed also tests whether voltage causes a change. In several sea urchin species, an unfertilized egg is negative inside. After one sperm fuses, voltage swings positive, and a second rarely enters. Suppose you clamp an egg at any voltage, then add sperm. What two results would show positive voltage blocks entry?
scenes.caption: Holding voltage fixed also tests whether voltage causes a change. In several sea urchin species, an unfertilized egg is negative inside. After one sperm fuses, voltage swings positive, and a second rarely enters. Suppose you clamp an egg at any voltage, then add sperm. What two results would show positive voltage blocks entry?
scenes.visual: The cell cross-section morphs smoothly into a schematic unfertilized sea urchin egg with the same intracellular electrode inside and the trace resting negative. A first schematic sperm contacts the membrane; the voltage trace swings positive and a second approaching sperm turns away. Then the clamp lock re-engages on the unfertilized egg as the question card appears in large high-contrast text: 'What two results would show positive voltage blocks entry?'
scenes.narration: Holding voltage fixed also tests whether voltage causes a change. In several sea urchin species, an unfertilized egg is negative inside. After one sperm fuses, voltage swings positive, and a second rarely enters. Suppose you clamp an egg at any voltage, then add sperm. What two results would show positive voltage blocks entry?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause (4.5 seconds): the question remains clearly on screen above the schematic clamped sea urchin egg with two blank outcome slots labeled 'Hold positive' and 'Hold negative'. Slow ambient ion drift continues so the frame never looks dead.

scenes.tts: Timing alone cannot prove voltage is the barrier, so test both ways. First, hold an unfertilized egg positive before adding sperm; entry should fail. Second, hold it negative as sperm arrive; extra sperm should enter.
scenes.caption: Timing alone cannot prove voltage is the barrier, so test both ways. First, hold an unfertilized egg positive before adding sperm; entry should fail. Second, hold it negative as sperm arrive; extra sperm should enter.
scenes.visual: The two outcome slots beside the schematic clamped egg fill in as narrated: in 'Hold positive', the clamped trace stays flat in positive territory and approaching schematic sperm fail to enter; in 'Hold negative', the clamped trace stays flat in negative territory and multiple schematic sperm enter the egg.
scenes.narration: Timing alone cannot prove voltage is the barrier, so test both ways. First, hold an unfertilized egg positive before adding sperm; entry should fail. Second, hold it negative as sperm arrive; extra sperm should enter.

scenes.tts: Limits matter: one other sea urchin showed no electrical block, and reviews conclude mouse eggs use none. Fatt and Katz recorded small random blips inside frog muscle where the nerve ends. Move the electrode away from that endplate, and the blips shrink and fade. So they arise at the nerve ending, not the electrode.
scenes.caption: Limits matter: one other sea urchin showed no electrical block, and reviews conclude mouse eggs use none. Fatt and Katz recorded small random blips inside frog muscle where the nerve ends. Move the electrode away from that endplate, and the blips shrink and fade. So they arise at the nerve ending, not the electrode.
scenes.visual: First, compact high-contrast badges beside the schematic egg note 'One other sea urchin: no electrical block' and 'Mouse egg: block not electrical (reviews)'. Then the same cell-and-electrode world shifts into a schematic frog muscle fiber with a nerve ending touching the endplate; small irregular depolarization blips tick along the flat trace (tag 'Fatt & Katz'). As the electrode slides along the fiber away from the endplate, the blips visibly shrink and fade into the flat baseline.
scenes.narration: Limits matter: one other sea urchin showed no electrical block, and reviews conclude mouse eggs use none. Fatt and Katz recorded small random blips inside frog muscle where the nerve ends. Move the electrode away from that endplate, and the blips shrink and fade. So they arise at the nerve ending, not the electrode.

scenes.tts: In nineteen thirty-nine, Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley pushed an electrode down a squid giant axon. Theory said the impulse's voltage should stop near zero. Instead, at the peak of the action potential, the inside became positive.
scenes.caption: In 1939, Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley pushed an electrode down a squid giant axon. Theory said the impulse's voltage should stop near zero. Instead, at the peak of the action potential, the inside became positive.
scenes.visual: Carried electrode-and-trace world: an electrode slides down inside a wide schematic squid giant axon. A dashed line at 0 mV is tagged 'expected stop'; the schematic action-potential trace shoots past it into positive territory (label 'Hodgkin & Huxley, 1939').
scenes.narration: In 1939, Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley pushed an electrode down a squid giant axon. Theory said the impulse's voltage should stop near zero. Instead, at the peak of the action potential, the inside became positive.

scenes.tts: In nineteen seventy-seven, Hudspeth and Corey pushed the sensing hair bundles of bullfrog inner-ear cells while recording inside. The voltage grew smoothly with distance, up to about fifteen millivolts, in that frog preparation.
scenes.caption: In 1977, Hudspeth and Corey pushed the sensing hair bundles of bullfrog inner-ear cells while recording inside. The voltage grew smoothly with distance, up to about 15 mV, in that frog preparation.
scenes.visual: Same layout: a fine probe nudges a schematic bullfrog hair bundle by increasing distances while the intracellular electrode records a smooth graded rise that levels off at a mark labeled 'up to ~15 mV (frog prep)' (label 'Hudspeth & Corey, 1977'; trace shape schematic).
scenes.narration: In 1977, Hudspeth and Corey pushed the sensing hair bundles of bullfrog inner-ear cells while recording inside. The voltage grew smoothly with distance, up to about 15 mV, in that frog preparation.

scenes.tts: In nineteen eighty, Brown and DiFrancesco studied rabbit sinoatrial node tissue, the heart's pacemaker. They recorded a current that flows over the pacemaker voltage range, and adrenaline increased it. Read voltage inside; hold it steady to expose the currents.
scenes.caption: In 1980, Brown and DiFrancesco studied rabbit sinoatrial node tissue, the heart's pacemaker. They recorded a current that flows over the pacemaker voltage range, and adrenaline increased it. Read voltage inside; hold it steady to expose the currents.
scenes.visual: Same clamped cell-and-trace world morphs to schematic rabbit sinoatrial node tissue (label 'Brown & DiFrancesco, 1980'): a stepped voltage clamp spans the pacemaker voltage range while the schematic current trace below grows noticeably larger when an 'Adrenaline' pulse sweeps across the bath. On the closing line, the electrode, fixed voltage line, and active current trace glow together in crisp symmetry.
scenes.narration: In 1980, Brown and DiFrancesco studied rabbit sinoatrial node tissue, the heart's pacemaker. They recorded a current that flows over the pacemaker voltage range, and adrenaline increased it. Read voltage inside; hold it steady to expose the currents.

scenes.visual: Clean dark end card holding for 3.5 seconds with the take-home rule centered in large high-contrast type: 'Record voltage from inside; hold it fixed to measure the currents.'
